documents.example: An investor who sells a large investment position in October, realizing a big capital gain, may need to make an estimated tax payment for that specific quarter rather than waiting until the following April to settle up.

documents.definition: Gross income is all the money, goods, services, and property a taxpayer receives during the year that must be reported for tax purposes, before any deductions or exemptions are applied. It generally includes both earned income (like wages) and certain unearned income (like interest).
documents.example: A worker's gross income includes their salary plus any taxable interest earned on a savings account, before subtracting deductions.

documents.definition: Adjusted gross income is gross income reduced by specific allowable adjustments, such as a deductible IRA contribution or student loan interest. AGI is a key subtotal on a tax return because many deductions, credits, and eligibility limits are based on it.
documents.example: Two taxpayers with the same gross income can end up with different AGIs if only one of them made a deductible retirement account contribution.

documents.definition: Filing status determines the tax rates, standard deduction, and some credit eligibility that apply to a return. The main U.S. options are single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, and qualifying widow(er), each with its own eligibility rules.
documents.example: A married couple can usually choose to file jointly (combining income and deductions on one return) or separately, depending on which produces a better result for their situation.

documents.definition: The standard deduction is a fixed amount that reduces the income subject to tax, available to taxpayers who don't itemize. The amount varies by filing status, age, blindness, and dependency status, and generally adjusts over time.
documents.example: A single filer who has few itemizable expenses will usually take the standard deduction instead of listing individual deductions.

documents.definition: Exemptions historically reduced the income subject to tax for the taxpayer, their spouse, and each qualifying dependent. Personal exemptions cover the taxpayer and spouse, while dependency exemptions cover qualifying children or relatives; current law and amounts can change significantly, so up-to-date rules should be checked.
documents.example: A household could once reduce their taxable income by an exemption amount for each qualifying child living with them.

documents.definition: A tax deduction is an amount, often a personal or business expense, that reduces the income subject to tax before the tax is calculated. Deductions lower the base the tax rate is applied to, unlike a credit, which reduces the tax itself.
documents.example: Contributing to a deductible traditional IRA reduces the income on which tax is calculated for that year.

documents.definition: A tax credit is a dollar-for-dollar reduction of the tax owed, applied after the tax has already been calculated. Because it reduces the tax bill directly rather than the income it's based on, a credit is generally more valuable than a deduction of the same dollar amount.
documents.example: A $500 tax credit reduces a tax bill by exactly $500, while a $500 deduction only reduces it by $500 times the taxpayer's marginal rate.

documents.definition: A nonrefundable credit can only reduce a taxpayer's liability to zero; any leftover credit amount is lost. A refundable credit can reduce liability below zero, with the excess paid to the taxpayer as part of their refund.
documents.example: If a $600 nonrefundable credit is applied against a $400 tax bill, $200 of the credit is unused; a refundable credit in the same situation could instead add $200 to the refund.

documents.definition: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a refundable credit for certain workers with earned income below a set limit, designed to supplement the income of lower- and moderate-income workers. Eligibility and the credit amount depend on income, filing status, and number of qualifying children.
documents.example: A working parent with modest earnings and qualifying children may receive a larger credit than a similarly-paid worker without children.

documents.definition: Withholding is the money an employer holds back from an employee's paycheck and forwards to the government, generally as an advance payment toward the employee's expected tax liability for the year. The amount withheld is credited against the tax owed when the return is filed.
documents.example: An employee's Form W-4 tells their employer how much income tax to withhold from each paycheck.

documents.definition: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer when the total tax payments made during the year, through withholding and/or estimated payments, exceed the total tax actually owed.
documents.example: A taxpayer who had more withheld from each paycheck than their eventual tax liability receives the difference back as a refund after filing.

documents.definition: Tax liability is the total amount of tax a taxpayer owes for the year, before accounting for how much has already been paid through withholding or estimated payments. Comparing tax liability to total payments determines whether the taxpayer owes more or receives a refund.
documents.example: A taxpayer's tax liability might be $8,000, but if $8,500 was withheld over the year, they receive a $500 refund.

documents.definition: A progressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from higher-income taxpayers than from lower-income taxpayers, typically through graduated brackets. The U.S. federal income tax is structured this way.
documents.example: Under a progressive system, a higher earner's last dollars of income are taxed at a higher rate than a lower earner's income.

documents.definition: A regressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from lower-income taxpayers than from higher-income taxpayers. Flat-rate sales and excise taxes are often cited as regressive in effect, since lower earners tend to spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods.
documents.example: A flat sales tax on groceries can take up a bigger share of a lower-income household's budget than a higher-income household's budget.

documents.definition: A proportional, or flat, tax takes the same percentage of income from every income group, regardless of how much a taxpayer earns.
documents.example: A flat 10% income tax would take the same 10% share from both a low-income and a high-income taxpayer.

documents.term: Payroll Taxes (Social Security and Medicare / FICA)
documents.definition: Payroll taxes are taxes collected from wages to fund specific programs, chiefly Social Security and Medicare. In the U.S. these are jointly known as FICA taxes and are typically split between employee and employer.
documents.example: A portion of every paycheck is withheld for Social Security and Medicare, separate from federal income tax withholding.

documents.definition: Self-employment tax is the self-employed equivalent of Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes, since independent workers don't have an employer to share the cost. It is calculated on self-employment profit rather than on wages.
documents.example: A freelancer who nets $50,000 in self-employment profit owes self-employment tax on that profit in addition to regular income tax.

documents.definition: Tax avoidance is the legal use of allowed deductions, credits, and account types to reduce a tax bill. Tax evasion is illegal: failing to pay, or deliberately underpaying, taxes that are actually owed.
documents.example: Contributing to a tax-advantaged retirement account to lower taxable income is tax avoidance; hiding income from the IRS is tax evasion.

documents.definition: Voluntary compliance is the principle that the U.S. tax system relies on taxpayers to report their income honestly, calculate their own liability correctly, and file on time, rather than the government calculating each person's tax for them.
documents.example: Filing an accurate return by the deadline, without being individually audited first, is an example of voluntary compliance in action.

documents.definition: Income tax is a tax governments levy on the money people and businesses earn, covering both earned income (wages, salaries, tips, commissions) and unearned income (interest, dividends, and similar). In the U.S., the federal government collects a federal income tax to fund national programs such as defense and law enforcement, and many states and some cities levy their own income tax on top of it.
documents.example: An employee who earns wages and also collects interest on a savings account owes income tax on both the wages and the interest.
